newsitem.title: ITALY: Political wrangles cloud Italy telecoms sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Political wrangles cloud Italy telecoms sell-off.

text.p: Italy's next big privatisation, the sale of telecoms holding Stet ran into trouble on Tuesday when a parliamentary commission abandoned work on a watchdog body for the sector because of political filibustering.
The Public Works commission of the Senate (upper house) indefinitely postponed consideration of the bill because of a welter of cross-party amendments, parliamentary sources said.
The commission was due to have begun examining some 400 amendments and 6,000 sub-amendments to the bill, which has been stalled for months, but it abandoned work and set no new date.
Stet shares ended 16 lire down at 5,438 on the Milan bourse.

The watchdog, which will regulate the privatised telecoms and television sectors, must be set up before the sell-off of the state's 64 percent holding in Stet, which the government has announced will take place by March 31 next year.
Any delay would be a setback for the government after last weekend's successful flotation of a second tranche in energy giant ENI.

It would also pose political problems as many of the objections come from hard-left Communist Refoundation, the party Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left coalition relies upon for a majority in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house).

Because of that, commentators say Prodi would be practically unable to call a confidence vote on the issue, as he has done twice in the past week to ram through legislation snarled by opposition filibustering.
Any attempt to get the opposition to help pass the bill into law would also incur the wrath of the hard-left.
Communist Refoundation is ideologically opposed to the Stet privatisation and has presented nearly 100 amendments.
Italy needs to complete the Stet sale to honour promises to the European Union under a deal which allowed it to bail out a bankrupt state holding company if it sold Stet by year-end.
Brussels has already given Rome a six month extension on the Stet sale, but the government is increasingly alarmed that even this new timetable might prove impossible.
Italy's stop-go asset sale programme has been badly hit by four years of constant political upheaval but Prodi has said the government plans to stick to its timetable.
He said last week he hoped the watchdog bill would be approved by parliament in coming weeks.

Michele Lauria, Undersecretary at the Post and Telecommunications Ministry, appealed earlier on Tuesday for wide-ranging political clarification to clear away obstacles erected by political parties to block the bill.
But he insisted: "The privatisation of Stet nevertheless remains set for the first months of 1997."
